catalog_quote: It appears that Lai treats the syllable final position on a par with the word final position. This may be a consequence of the morphology of Lai. A majority of the polysyllabic words in my lexicon are compound words, where each syllable is a word. Stress Stress in Lai falls invariably on the last syllable. [Conclusion, p. 19:] In this paper I have attempted to describe the sound system of Lai by providing an inventory of the phonemes and allophones of the language, including their distribution. Additionally, I discussed a number of its interesting phonetic characteristics: ... •an undeviating stress pattern

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the word, with no exceptions stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: based on a ~300-word lexicon elicited from one speaker (Kenneth VanBik, born and raised in Haka, Chin State) plus STEDT data; the author notes most polysyllabic words in her lexicon are compounds of monosyllabic words. One-sentence statement with no examples or instrumental support. The language is tonal: Hyman & VanBik (2002, 2004) describe a three-way tone contrast on largely monosyllabic words and phrase-level 'left-prominence', and do not mention word stress at all.
new_statements.identity_note: Melnik 1997 describes the Lai of Haka (Hakha) town, Chin State, Myanmar, from a single Haka-born consultant (Kenneth VanBik); this is the Hakha Lai variety = haka1240 itself, not a divergent dialect. Newland 1897 calls the same variety the 'Baungshe dialect'. Lalremzami 2013 (unread) covers Haka and Khuafo varieties spoken in Mizoram, India.

sources.note: p. 16, heading 'Stress': 'Stress in Lai falls invariably on the last syllable.' Conclusion p. 19 lists 'an undeviating stress pattern' among the language's characteristics. No examples, no secondary stress, no exceptions. Data: ~300-word lexicon elicited from one Haka-born speaker (Kenneth VanBik) plus STEDT data; most polysyllabic words in the lexicon are compounds whose syllables are words.
